title: Networking Domain 4: Network Security, Hardening, VPNs & Attacks (14%)
overview: Covers Zero Trust, AAA/802.1X NAC, Firewalls/ACLs, IPSec/TLS VPNs, and Layer 2/Layer 3 network attacks.
art: [ NGFW / IDS / IPS ]                         • VLAN Hopping  -> Mitigate: Disable DTP
├─ Screened Subnet (DMZ) -> Web/DNS        • Evil Twin AP   -> Mitigate: 802.1X/WPA3
└─ Internal LAN -> 802.1X NAC + Zero Trust • DDoS / SYN Flood -> Mitigate: Rate Limit

1.label: Zero Trust Architecture, AAA & 802.1X NAC
1.what: Modern security assumes the internal network is already hostile ('Never Trust, Always Verify') and authenticates every user and device before granting access.
1.exam_facts: AAA: Authentication (who are you?), Authorization (what can you access?), Accounting (logging what you did). Protocols: RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813, encrypts password only, standard for Wi-Fi/VPN) vs TACACS+ (TCP 49, Cisco proprietary, encrypts entire packet, separates AAA for router/switch admin). 802.1X (NAC): Uses EAP, Supplicant (client), Authenticator (switch/AP), and Authentication Server (RADIUS) to quarantine non-compliant devices into a remediation VLAN.
1.troubleshoot: If a workstation gets stuck on a Guest/Remediation VLAN instead of the Corporate VLAN, check its 802.1X machine certificate or RADIUS server reachability.

2.label: Firewalls, ACLs, Screened Subnets (DMZ) & VPNs
2.what: Controls traffic boundaries between trusted internal networks, semi-trusted public servers, and remote users.
2.exam_facts: ACLs process rules TOP-TO-BOTTOM and end with an invisible 'Implicit Deny All'—always put specific permit rules above broad deny rules! Screened Subnet (formerly DMZ): Isolates public-facing servers (web/email) between two firewalls so a breach doesn't reach the internal LAN. VPNs: IPSec (Layer 3, uses AH for integrity and ESP for encryption+integrity, Tunnel vs Transport mode) vs SSL/TLS VPN (Layer 4-7, port 443, easy client/browser remote access).
2.troubleshoot: If you add a new 'Permit' rule to the bottom of an existing ACL and traffic is still blocked, you probably placed it *below* an explicit 'Deny Any' line!

3.label: Layer 2 Switch Attacks & Hardening Mitigations
3.what: Attacks targeting Ethernet frames, MAC tables, and VLAN boundaries on the local switch.
3.exam_facts: MAC Flooding (overflows switch CAM table so it fails open as a hub) -> Mitigate with Port Security (sticky MAC / max MAC limit). ARP Spoofing/Poisoning (attacker sends fake ARP replies for Man-in-the-Middle) -> Mitigate with Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI). Rogue DHCP Server / DHCP Starvation -> Mitigate with DHCP Snooping (sets trusted uplink ports vs untrusted client ports). VLAN Hopping (Switch Spoofing / Double Tagging) -> Mitigate by disabling DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) and changing Native VLAN away from VLAN 1.
3.troubleshoot: Enable BPDU Guard on all user access ports so plugging an unauthorized switch into a wall jack immediately shuts the port down (`err-disabled`) instead of hijacking Spanning Tree.

4.label: Wireless, DNS & Volumetric Attacks (DoS/DDoS)
4.what: Attacks aimed at hijacking wireless clients, poisoning name resolution, or exhausting bandwidth/CPU.
4.exam_facts: Evil Twin (rogue AP broadcasting the exact same SSID to steal credentials) & Deauthentication Flood (spoofed management frames kicking clients off Wi-Fi—mitigated by 802.11w Protected Management Frames / WPA3). DNS Poisoning (corrupts DNS cache to redirect users to fake sites—mitigated by DNSSEC). On-Path Attack (formerly Man-in-the-Middle). MAC Spoofing (cloning an allowed MAC address to bypass weak MAC filtering).
4.troubleshoot: Never rely on 'SSID Hiding' or 'MAC Filtering' as real wireless security—both can be bypassed in seconds with basic packet sniffing.
